name: The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time?
title: The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time?
answer: A time study checks whether an AI tool actually saves teachers time by measuring how long key tasks took before the tool and how long they take after, including the time spent checking and correcting AI output. It matters because schools often adopt these tools on the promise of saved time without ever verifying it, and the evidence shows savings cannot be assumed.

sections.body: Schools frequently bring in AI tools expecting teachers to gain time, yet almost none measure whether that happens. A time study answers the question directly: teachers record how long tasks such as planning a week of lessons or grading a set of essays take before the tool arrives, then record the same tasks again after a few weeks of use. The difference is the real saving, and it must count the extra time spent reviewing and fixing what the AI produces. The study also asks where any saved time actually goes, because time that is quietly absorbed by other demands disappears rather than helping teachers. This gives leaders a factual basis for deciding whether a tool is worth keeping and how to protect whatever time it frees.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The study is run simply, with teachers logging tasks and their times each week in a few minutes, for example through a Google Form. Before a tool is introduced, they note the duration of regular work like planning a week of lessons or grading a set of essays, and after a few weeks with the tool they record the same tasks again. They also note what they did with any time saved, whether that was more small group teaching, more feedback conferences, or leaving earlier. The book describes this as a general approach for schools rather than giving separate versions by grade band, though the primary school study it cites shows saved time being absorbed by other demands. Results are shared with teachers as a way to learn, not to judge them.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research findings rather than treating it as settled practice. A review of 63 studies of automatic feedback found that many showed benefits for students, but 46 percent found no evidence that it eased instructors' workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). The book states plainly that time savings cannot be assumed. It also cites a primary school study finding that saved time was often absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets clear limits on how a time study should be used. The results belong to teachers and should be shared with them, never used to judge or monitor individuals, because the purpose is to learn whether tools help rather than to watch teachers. The measurement itself must be honest, counting the time spent checking and fixing AI output rather than only the time the tool appears to remove. Leaders also carry a decision the data cannot make for them: once they know where saved time goes, they must act to protect it, since the primary school study showed it is often absorbed by other demands. Nothing in the study removes the teacher's own judgement about whether a tool is worth the time it costs.
